***Stranger Things*** is an American television series created by [the Duffer Brothers](/wiki/The_Duffer_Brothers "The Duffer Brothers") for [Netflix](/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"). Produced by Monkey Massacre Productions and [21 Laps Entertainment](/wiki/21_Laps_Entertainment "21 Laps Entertainment"), the [first season](/wiki/Stranger_Things_season_1 "Stranger Things season 1") was released on Netflix on July 15, 2016. The [second](/wiki/Stranger_Things_season_2 "Stranger Things season 2") and [third](/wiki/Stranger_Things_season_3 "Stranger Things season 3") seasons followed in October 2017 and July 2019, respectively, and the [fourth season](/wiki/Stranger_Things_season_4 "Stranger Things season 4") was released in two parts in May and July 2022. The [fifth and final season](/wiki/Stranger_Things_season_5 "Stranger Things season 5") was released in three volumes, including the [finale](/wiki/Chapter_Eight:_The_Rightside_Up "Chapter Eight: The Rightside Up"), in November and December 2025. The show combines elements of horror, [science fiction](/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction"), [mystery](/wiki/Mystery_fiction "Mystery fiction"), [coming-of-age](/wiki/Coming-of-age_story "Coming-of-age story"), and [drama](/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)").

Set in the [1980s](/wiki/1980s "1980s"), the series centers on the residents of the fictional small town of Hawkins, [Indiana](/wiki/Indiana "Indiana"), after a young girl with [psychokinetic abilities](/wiki/Psychokinesis "Psychokinesis"), named [Eleven](/wiki/Eleven_(Stranger_Things) "Eleven (Stranger Things)"), inadvertently creates a wormhole known as the [Upside Down](/wiki/Upside_Down_(Stranger_Things) "Upside Down (Stranger Things)"), at a nearby secretive government research facility called Hawkins Lab, connecting Earth to a hostile realm called the Abyss. fanoutqa_024814.x:
Persian cat :: Health :: Life span :: chunk_0014
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Purr_Lexus_Persian_Kitty_January_3_2015_19_years_and_6_months_old.jpg/250px-Purr_Lexus_Persian_Kitty_January_3_2015_19_years_and_6_months_old.jpg)](/wiki/File:Purr_Lexus_Persian_Kitty_January_3_2015_19_years_and_6_months_old.jpg)

A 19.5-year-old black tabby and white Persian. Such longevity is rare in this breed.[[68]](#cite_note-auto-68)

The lifespan of Persian cats varies depending on their country. Pet insurance data from Sweden puts the median lifespan of cats from the Persian group (Persians, Chinchilla, Himalayan and Exotic) at just above 12.5 years, while most cats live until they are about 15 years old. 76% of this group lived for 10 years or more and 52% lived for 12.5 years or more.[[68]](#cite_note-auto-68) A 2015 study looking at veterinary clinic data from England shows an average lifespan of 14.1.[[69]](#cite_note-69) A 2024 UK study found a life expectancy of 10.93 years for the Persian (9.63–12.23) compared to an overall of 11.74 years (11.61–11.87).[[70]](#cite_note-70)

Arata Isozaki :: Biography :: chunk_0001
Isozaki was born in Oita on the island of Kyushu and grew up in the era of [postwar Japan](/wiki/Postwar_Japan "Postwar Japan"),[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4) the eldest of four children of Toji and Tetsu Isozaki. His father was a prominent businessman.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) In 1945, he witnessed the destruction of [Hiroshima](/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima") on the shore opposite his hometown.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) When he accepted the [Pritzker Prize](/wiki/Pritzker_Architecture_Prize "Pritzker Architecture Prize") in 2019 he stated: "There was no architecture, no buildings, and not even a city. So my first experience of architecture was the void of architecture, and I began to consider how people might rebuild their homes and cities."[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2)

Isozaki completed his schooling at the [Oita Prefecture](/wiki/%C5%8Cita_(city) "Ōita (city)") Oita Uenogaoka High School (erstwhile Oita Junior High School). In 1954, he graduated from the [University of Tokyo](/wiki/University_of_Tokyo "University of Tokyo") majoring in Architecture and Engineering. He completed a doctoral program in architecture from the same university in 1961.[[1]](#cite_note-arata-1) Isozaki also worked under [Kenzo Tange](/wiki/Kenzo_Tange "Kenzo Tange") before establishing his firm in 1963.[[1]](#cite_note-arata-1)

Isozaki's early projects were influenced by European experiences with a style mixed between "New Brutalism" and "[Metabolist Architecture](/wiki/Metabolism_(architecture) "Metabolism (architecture)")" (Oita Medical Hall, 1959–1960), according to Reyner Banham. His style continued to evolve with buildings such as the Fujimi Country Club (1973–74) and Kitakyushu Central Library (1973–74). Later he developed a more modernistic style with buildings such as the [Art Tower of Mito](/wiki/Art_Tower_Mito "Art Tower Mito") (1986–90) and [Domus-Casa del Hombre](/wiki/Domus_(museum) "Domus (museum)") (1991–1995) in [Galicia, Spain](/wiki/Galicia,_Spain "Galicia, Spain"). Main articles: [Earth's orbit](/wiki/Earth%27s_orbit "Earth's orbit") and [Earth's location](/wiki/Earth%27s_location "Earth's location")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Seasons1.svg/250px-Seasons1.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Seasons1.svg)

Exaggerated illustration of Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun, marking that the orbital extreme points ([apoapsis](/wiki/Apoapsis "Apoapsis") and [periapsis](/wiki/Periapsis "Periapsis")) are not the same as the four seasonal extreme points, the [equinox](/wiki/Equinox "Equinox") and [solstice](/wiki/Solstice "Solstice")

Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance is about 150 million km (93 million mi). This makes Earth the third-closest planet to the Sun and part of the [inner Solar System](/wiki/Inner_Solar_System "Inner Solar System"). Its orbital distance is the basis for the [astronomical unit](/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") (AU) and is equal to roughly 8.3 [light minutes](/wiki/Light_minute "Light minute") or 380 times [Earth's distance to the Moon](/wiki/Lunar_distance "Lunar distance"). Earth orbits the Sun every 365.2564 mean [solar days](/wiki/Solar_day "Solar day"), or one [sidereal year](/wiki/Sidereal_year "Sidereal year"). With an apparent movement of the Sun in Earth's sky at a rate of about 1°/day eastward, which is one apparent Sun or Moon diameter every 12 hours. Due to this motion, on average it takes 24 hours—a solar day—for Earth to complete a full rotation about its axis so that the Sun returns to the [meridian](/wiki/Meridian_(astronomy) "Meridian (astronomy)"), slightly longer than the sidereal day.

The orbital speed of Earth averages at 29.7827 km/s (107,218 km/h; 66,622 mph), which is fast enough to travel a distance equal to Earth's diameter, about 12,742 km (7,918 mi), in seven minutes, and the distance from Earth to the Moon, 384,400 km (238,855 mi), in about 3.5 hours.[[3]](#cite_note-earth_fact_sheet-5) Viewed from a vantage point above the Sun and Earth's north poles, Earth orbits in a counterclockwise direction about the Sun. [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/UBC_President_Santa_Ono.jpg/250px-UBC_President_Santa_Ono.jpg)](/wiki/File:UBC_President_Santa_Ono.jpg)

Ono speaking at a public event in 2018

Ono received an honorary doctorate degree from [Chiba University](/wiki/Chiba_University "Chiba University") in Japan in 2016[[123]](#cite_note-123) and an honorary [doctor of divinity](/wiki/Doctor_of_Divinity "Doctor of Divinity") from the [Vancouver School of Theology](/wiki/Vancouver_School_of_Theology "Vancouver School of Theology") of the University of British Columbia in 2020.[[124]](#cite_note-124) In 2017, he received a Professional Achievement Award from the University of Chicago Alumni Association.[[125]](#cite_note-125) Ono was elected as a fellow of the [Canadian Academy of Health Sciences](/wiki/Canadian_Academy_of_Health_Sciences "Canadian Academy of Health Sciences") in 2017,[[126]](#cite_note-126) He was elected as a member of the [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "American Academy of Arts and Sciences") in 2022.[[127]](#cite_note-127) He was elected as a member of the [National Academy of Medicine](/wiki/National_Academy_of_Medicine "National Academy of Medicine") in the United States in October 2024.[[128]](#cite_note-128)

Princeton University's endowment of $37 billion (per 2021 figures) was ranked as the [fourth](/wiki/List_of_US_colleges_and_universities_by_endowment "List of US colleges and universities by endowment") largest endowment in the United States,[[241]](#cite_note-244) and it had the greatest per-student endowment in the world at over $4.4 million per student.[[242]](#cite_note-245)[[243]](#cite_note-246) The endowment is sustained through continued donations and is maintained by investment advisers.[[244]](#cite_note-247) Princeton's operating budget is over $2 billion per year, with 50% going to academic departments and programs, 33% to administrative and student service departments, 10% to financial aid departments, and 7% to the [Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory](/wiki/Princeton_Plasma_Physics_Laboratory "Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory").[[245]](#cite_note-248)

Mechanism of 2011 Tōhoku earthquake

This megathrust earthquake was a recurrence of the mechanism of the earlier [869 Sanriku earthquake](/wiki/869_Sanriku_earthquake "869 Sanriku earthquake"), which has been estimated as having a magnitude of at least 8.4 Mw, which also created a large tsunami that inundated the Sendai plain.[[38]](#cite_note-w-39)[[74]](#cite_note-75)[[75]](#cite_note-76) Three tsunami deposits have been identified within the [Holocene](/wiki/Holocene "Holocene") sequence of the plain, all formed within the last 3,000 years, suggesting an 800 to 1,100 year recurrence interval for large tsunamigenic earthquakes. In 2001 it was reckoned that there was a high likelihood of a large tsunami hitting the Sendai plain as more than 1,100 years had then elapsed.[[76]](#cite_note-Minoura-77) In 2007, the probability of an earthquake with a magnitude of Mw 8.1–8.3 was estimated as 99% within the following 30 years.[[77]](#cite_note-Satake-78)

This earthquake occurred where the [Pacific plate](/wiki/Pacific_plate "Pacific plate") is [subducting](/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") under the plate beneath northern Honshu.[[66]](#cite_note-NYTimes-Chang2011-03-13-67)[[56]](#cite_note-grauniad-57) The Pacific plate, which moves at a rate of 8 to 9 cm (3.1 to 3.5 in) per year, dips under Honshu's underlying plate, building large amounts of [elastic energy](/wiki/Elastic_energy "Elastic energy"). This motion pushes the upper plate down until the accumulated stress causes a seismic slip-rupture event. The break caused the sea floor to rise by several meters.[[56]](#cite_note-grauniad-57) The magnitude of this earthquake was a surprise to some seismologists.[[78]](#cite_note-:2-79) A quake of this magnitude usually has a rupture length of at least 500 km (310 mi) and generally requires a long, relatively straight fault surface. fanoutqa_023022.t: Doug McMillon :: Career :: CEO of Walmart, Inc. (2014–2026) :: part 02 :: chunk_0004
fanoutqa_023022.x:
Doug McMillon :: Career :: CEO of Walmart, Inc. (2014–2026) :: part 02 :: chunk_0004
In December 2016, McMillon joined a business forum assembled by then president-elect [Donald Trump](/wiki/Donald_J._Trump "Donald J. Trump") to provide strategic and policy advice on economic issues.[[37]](#cite_note-37) In August 2017, McMillon wrote a rebuke of President Trump's response to the violent protests, despite Trump’s condemnation of alt-right protestors in [Charlottesville](/wiki/Charlottesville,_Virginia "Charlottesville, Virginia"), Virginia in an email to all employees and on the internal company website viewable by the public. The statement said that Trump, "missed a critical opportunity to help bring our country together". A company spokesman said McMillon would continue to serve on a presidential advisory council on economic development.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

In September 2019, McMillon announced that the company would no longer sell ammunition used for handguns and military-style weapons. This policy update came as a result of the [mass shooting](/wiki/2019_El_Paso_shooting "2019 El Paso shooting") which took place at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas in August 2019. McMillon's actions to create a dialogue and take actions around the issue, set a new precedent for how corporations and their leaders address these matters.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

In 2023, McMillon's total compensation from Walmart was $27 million, or 976 times the median Walmart employee pay for that year.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

In November 2025, Walmart announced McMillon would retire as CEO in January 2026 after almost 12 years as CEO and over 40 years with the company.[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-42)[[43]](#cite_note-43) At the time of the announcement, McMillon had overseen a 400%+ rise in Walmart shares, equating to more than $576 billion in [market capitalization](/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization").[[44]](#cite_note-44)

McMillon lives with his wife, Shelley, in Bentonville, Arkansas.[[23]](#cite_note-CreswellTabuchi15-23) They have two sons.[[10]](#cite_note-USAToday10-10)

See also: [Eric Lindros trade](/wiki/Eric_Lindros_trade "Eric Lindros trade")

Prior to the [1991–92 season](/wiki/1991%E2%80%9392_NHL_season "1991–92 NHL season"), the Flyers acquired [Rod Brind'Amour](/wiki/Rod_Brind%27Amour "Rod Brind'Amour") from St. Louis. Brind'Amour led the Flyers in goals (33), assists (44) and points (77) in his first season with the club. With Ron Sutter gone to St. Louis in the Brind'Amour trade, [Rick Tocchet](/wiki/Rick_Tocchet "Rick Tocchet") was named team captain. As the Flyers continued to flounder, Paul Holmgren was fired midway through the season and replaced by [Bill Dineen](/wiki/Bill_Dineen_(ice_hockey) "Bill Dineen (ice hockey)"), father of Flyer [Kevin Dineen](/wiki/Kevin_Dineen "Kevin Dineen"). On February 19, the Flyers and Pittsburgh made a major five-player deal which featured Tocchet – who never grew comfortably into the role of captain – heading to Pittsburgh and [Mark Recchi](/wiki/Mark_Recchi "Mark Recchi") coming to Philadelphia. Recchi recorded 27 points in his first 22 games as a Flyer, but the team missed the playoffs for the third consecutive year, due in large part to an awful road record (10–26–4). With Tocchet traded, the Flyers remained without a captain until Kevin Dineen was named to the post in 1993–94, and instead went with three alternate captains.

In June 1992, the Flyers persuaded Bobby Clarke to return to the team as senior vice president after [Jay Snider](/wiki/Jay_T._Snider "Jay T. Snider") won the hard-fought [arbitration battle](/wiki/Eric_Lindros_trade "Eric Lindros trade") for [1991](/wiki/1991_NHL_entry_draft "1991 NHL entry draft") first overall pick [Eric Lindros](/wiki/Eric_Lindros "Eric Lindros") against the Rangers. It was determined that Quebec had made a deal with the Flyers before making a deal with the Rangers. The regular icosahedron inside the regular dodecahedron

The [dual polyhedron](/wiki/Dual_polyhedron "Dual polyhedron") of a dodecahedron is the [regular icosahedron](/wiki/Regular_icosahedron "Regular icosahedron"). One property of the dual polyhedron generally is that the original polyhedron and its dual share the same [three-dimensional symmetry group](/wiki/Point_groups_in_three_dimensions "Point groups in three dimensions"). In the case of the regular dodecahedron, it has the same symmetry as the regular icosahedron, the [icosahedral symmetry](/wiki/Icosahedral_symmetry "Icosahedral symmetry")

Belichick was acquired in a "trade" with the rival [New York Jets](/wiki/New_York_Jets "New York Jets").[[163]](#cite_note-168) Belichick did not want to be under [Bill Parcells](/wiki/Bill_Parcells "Bill Parcells")' authority there in 2000, with uncertainty of his role once their owner, [Leon Hess](/wiki/Leon_Hess "Leon Hess"), died. The initial promise was that Belichick would've been granted extreme authority over all of the Jets executive decisions, but when Hess died Parcells overruled the stipulation with loopholes, so he would remain in control as general manager, leading to Belichick's infamous resignation in 2000. Parcells, a two winning Super Bowl champion coach with the [New York Giants](/wiki/New_York_Giants "New York Giants") (also was an assistant with the Patriots in the early 1980s), had joined New England's staff for the 1993 season to help resurrect the franchise from its dark early 1990s days but had conflicted interests with owner Robert Kraft.[[164]](#cite_note-169) In his last year with the Patriots in 1996, Parcells brought in his assistant head coach from his Giants days, Belichick, after being dismissed from coaching five seasons with the [Cleveland Browns](/wiki/Cleveland_Browns "Cleveland Browns"). Here, Kraft would plant the seeds of a bond between him and Belichick, as Belichick would often mediate issues between Kraft and Parcells. Although Belichick left in 1997 to once again be Parcells assistant in their Jets regime, cold feet about his long-term role there brought him back after negotiating with Kraft, even though he was still under contract with the Jets.[[165]](#cite_note-170) The Patriots had technically "tampered" in communicating with Belichick. For compensation, the Patriots gave the Jets their first-round pick in the [2000 NFL draft](/wiki/2000_NFL_draft "2000 NFL draft"), where even without their first-round pick, the Patriots would coincidentally draft [Tom Brady](/wiki/Tom_Brady "Tom Brady") in the sixth round, widely regarded as the greatest quarterback of all time and the NFL's greatest draft steal.[[166]](#cite_note-m162-17

The **Pacific War**, sometimes called the **Asia–Pacific War** or the **Pacific Theater**,[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurrayMillett2001143-44) was the [theater](/wiki/Theater_(warfare) "Theater (warfare)") of [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") fought between [Japan](/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") and the [Allies](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") in [East](/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") and [Southeast Asia](/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), the [Pacific](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") and [Indian Oceans](/wiki/Indian_Ocean "Indian Ocean"), and [Oceania](/wiki/Oceania "Oceania"). It was geographically the largest theater of the war, including the [Pacific Ocean theater](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean_theater_of_World_War_II "Pacific Ocean theater of World War II"), the [South West Pacific theater](/wiki/South_West_Pacific_theater_of_World_War_II "South West Pacific theater of World War II"), the [Second Sino-Japanese War](/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War"), and the brief [Soviet–Japanese War](/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Japanese_War "Soviet–Japanese War"), and included some of the [largest naval battles in history](/wiki/Largest_naval_battle_in_history "Largest naval battle in history"). As of the 2022 World Cup, 22 final tournaments have been held since the event's inception in 1930, and a total of 80 national teams have competed. [The trophy](/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup_Trophy "FIFA World Cup Trophy") has been won by eight national teams. With five wins, [Brazil](/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team") is the only team to have played in every tournament. The other World Cup winners are [Germany](/wiki/Germany_national_football_team "Germany national football team") and [Italy](/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team"), with four titles each; Argentina, with three titles; France and inaugural winner [Uruguay](/wiki/Uruguay_national_football_team "Uruguay national football team"), each with two titles; and [England](/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") and [Spain](/wiki/Spain_men%27s_national_football_team "Spain men's national football team"), with one title each.

The World Cup is globally regarded as the most prestigious association football competition, as well as the most widely viewed and followed sporting event in the world.[[2]](#cite_note-DobsonGoddard2006-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) The viewership of the [2018 World Cup](/wiki/2018_FIFA_World_Cup "2018 FIFA World Cup") was estimated to be 3.57 billion, close to half of the global population,[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) while the engagement with the 2022 World Cup was estimated to be 5 billion, with about 1.5 billion people watching [the final match](/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2022 FIFA World Cup final").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Eighteen countries have hosted the World Cup, most recently [Qatar](/wiki/Qatar "Qatar"), who hosted the 2022 event. The 2026 tournament will be jointly hosted by Canada, Mexico, and the United States, which will give Mexico the distinction of being the first country to host games in three World Cups.

Main article: [History of the FIFA World Cup](/wiki/History_of_the_FIFA_World_Cup "History of the FIFA World Cup")
